newsitem.title: USA: Amazon.com opens sharply higher after IPO.
newsitem.headline: Amazon.com opens sharply higher after IPO.

text.p: Shares of Internet bookseller Amazon.com opened 62 percent higher at their market debut on Thrusday after the company's initial public offering, one of the most closely-watched IPOs this year.

The shares opened at 29-1/4, up 11-1/4 from their IPO price of 18, which was sharply higher than expected. The strong demand sent the IPO price spiralling higher from Amazon's initial estimate of $12 to $14 a share. It also was able to offer more shares, three million, than its original offer of 2.5 million shares.

Deutsche Morgan Grenfell was the lead underwriter of the IPO with co-managers Alex. Brown Inc and Hambrecht & Quist. Amazon said it has granted the underwriters an option to purchase up to 450,000 additional shares from the company to covering over-allotments, if any.
IPO analysts had expected the two-year old Seattle company to garner strong premiums, especially since technology stocks have rebounded this month after slumping earlier in the year.

Amazon's sales are growing exponentially. It sold $15.7 million worth of books in 1996 and topped that in the first quarter this year, selling $16 million from its headquarters in a slightly run-down Seattle office building.
But it warned in its prosectus that such growth rates are probably "not sustainable" and it expects to incur "substantial operating losses for the foreseeable future."
With a cash infusion of roughly $50 million from the IPO, Amazon.com may be able to boost its profitability. It lost $3 million in the first quarter and $6 million last year.

The IPO comes as giant rival Barnes & Noble Inc turns up the competitive pressure. The 124-year-old chain, with more than 1,000 stores and $2.45 billion in sales last year, filed a suit seeking to block virtual rival Amazon.com from calling itself "The World's Largest Bookstore."
"Amazon is not a bookstore at all," Barnes & Noble complains in its lawsuit, filed in Federal court in New York.
"Rather, it is a book broker making use of the Internet exclusively to generate sales to the public," it said.
Amazon said in a statement it "intends to defend against the lawsuit vigorously" but is still evaluating the suit and is not in a position yet to comment on it has merit.
Barnes and Noble also launched its own Web site, boasting more than one million available books, the vast majority of which were being offered at prices that undercut Amazon's.
